A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S3 research work and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Shared content can be matched despite extensive reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original topic-model benchmarks, runtime measurements, preprocessing and noise analyses, and qualitative topic outputs in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 reports original empirical results across the retained and additional corpora, including model comparisons, scoring-variant evaluations, runtime measurements, and qualitative outputs.

M1.justification: v3 Section 3.1 retains the FastICA decomposition and original projection-based scoring, now called axial importance. It adds angular importance, W_jt/||W_j||, and combined importance, (W_jt)^3/||W_j||. These modify descriptive-word selection within the existing method; expanded whitening and inference explanations do not establish additional procedural changes.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on 75,000 StackExchange entries and 6,861 medical Wikipedia articles, broadening the represented document populations and domains. The original 20 Newsgroups, BBC News, and ArXiv ML corpora remain, as does the raw-versus-preprocessed 20 Newsgroups comparison.

E2.justification: FASTopic and ECRTM become evaluated comparators in quantitative, runtime, and qualitative comparisons, including v3 Tables 4–5 and Appendix I. All six earlier baselines remain. CombinedTM and CTMcombined denote the same comparator, rather than an additional method.

E3.justification: v3 introduces geometric-mean coherence and interpretability metrics and restricts encoder-dependent results in Figure 2 and Table 4 to sentence transformers. Runtime summaries use median ratios instead of mean percentage differences, and reported hardware changes from 64 Xeon Gold cores to 20 Xeon Silver cores. The four encoders, 10–50 topic settings, and top-10-word evaluation remain.

E4.justification: v3 Section 5.4 adds a systematic comparison of axial, angular, and combined importance, examining coherence/diversity tradeoffs and overlap between descriptive terms. It also analyzes FASTopic's encoder sensitivity. Existing preprocessing and noise analyses remain, while the five-topic ArXiv demonstration is retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports twice-standard-deviation summaries and highest-density intervals. v3's corpus tables omit those SD summaries, while Figure 2 adds bootstrap confidence intervals and Table 3 adds regression standard errors, p-values, and coefficient intervals. Sections 4.3 and 8.4 newly disclose one run per configuration and a single seed; they do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new corpora, baselines, and S3 variants, plus regression findings and changed appendix topic outputs. For example, Table 4 reports WikiMedical aggregate interpretability of 0.63 for Top2Vec versus 0.60 for all S3 variants. Revised runtime results have different reported hardware and aggregation, preventing direct same-setting performance comparisons.

T1.justification: v3 adds mathematical definitions for angular and combined importance and for geometric-mean coherence and interpretability in Sections 3.1 and 4.4. The ICA factorization and pseudoinverse relationship remain. These are limited formal extensions; neither version presents theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 removes v1's headline claim to be the first exclusively contextual model supporting multiple topics per document and its claim of state-of-the-art topic diversity. It instead claims near-perfect diversity and competitive coherence, while retaining the efficiency contribution and quantifying a median 4.5x advantage over BERTopic. These materially narrow the novelty and performance claims.

C2.justification: v1 flags possible repeated terms from its importance rule; v3 explains the salience/specificity tradeoff and recommends combined scoring. It adds a dimensionality-based explanation for FASTopic's behavior and substantive limitations concerning single-seed testing, untuned baselines, preprocessing evidence from one corpus, and unevaluated document-topic representations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies FASTopic and ECRTM hyperparameters and training settings, updates hardware information, explicitly states that timings exclude embedding computation, and explains whitening dimensionality reduction and unseen-document inference. The timing exclusion is newly documented, not an established change from v1. Existing core hyperparameters, code access, and MIT licensing remain.

R1.justification: A new Semantic Axes subsection discusses Yamagiwa et al. (2023) and Musil and Marecek (2024), distinguishing corpus-specific topic discovery from universal semantic dimensions. v3 also positions S3 against ECRTM and FASTopic and expands references supporting its discussions of evaluation limitations and hyperparameter tuning.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, and results undergo substantial rewriting and restructuring. Results are reorganized around preprocessing, stop words, encoders, and importance estimation; NPMI discussion moves into a dedicated appendix. Limitations and appendix organization expand substantially, beyond changes attributable solely to added experiments.

P2.justification: The existing overview schematic moves to the first page with an expanded caption. New figures present performance/speed rankings, scoring geometry, and encoder effects. Dataset and encoder tables are merged, comparison tables are restructured in the appendices, runtime plots switch to logarithmic axes, and nonalphabetical-term results become boxplots.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's limited empirical coverage through FASTopic/ECRTM comparisons, medical and StackExchange corpora, and direct investigation of the previously unresolved term-importance concern. It also clarifies research positioning and narrows headline claims to better reflect the evidence. Single-seed testing limits robustness, and changed timing conditions prevent direct speed comparisons across versions, but the broader evidence and more precise scope provide a substantial overall quality improvement.
